tagline: A gravel river road through basalt canyons and ranching country
intro: The South Fork John Day River Back Country Byway follows the river canyon for 50 miles, from Dayville to the northern boundary of Malheur National Forest. The drive passes through Columbia River basalt canyons, old-growth ponderosa pine, Douglas and white fir, and roadside willows. The gravel surface accommodates most passenger vehicles, though some sections narrow to a single vehicle’s width. The river’s recreational classification in the National Wild and Scenic River system covers 47 miles, a separate designation from the road’s Back Country Byway identity. Along the river, Izee Falls drops 56 feet, and the drive passes both Black Canyon Wilderness and Aldrich Mountain Wilderness Study Area.

At Dayville, a mid-19th-century wagon road connected The Dalles on the Columbia River with the gold mines near Canyon City. Beside the byway, Rockpile Ranch dates from the late 19th century and remains a working private ranch. Izee’s two-room schoolhouse served students until 1989; it now hosts community functions.

Begin at Dayville, where South Fork Road meets US 26 beside the confluence of the two rivers. Head south to Black Canyon East Trailhead, nine miles from town, then toward Izee, about 34 miles upstream, and the national forest boundary.
notice: Basalt canyon walls, ponderosa pine and roadside willows border the river drive.

moments.title: Dayville
moments.text: Two rivers and two roads meet at Dayville. The South Fork joins the John Day here, while north–south South Fork Road connects with east–west US 26. In the mid-19th century, a wagon road through Dayville connected The Dalles on the Columbia River with gold mines near Canyon City. It became The Dalles Military Road in about 1870. The byway begins with the turn south onto South Fork Road, following the smaller river toward Malheur National Forest. Dayville’s post office also changed locations: its original site lay three miles west of the present city.

moments.title: Black Canyon East Trailhead
moments.text: Nine miles south of Dayville, Black Canyon East Trailhead provides a way into the Black Canyon Wilderness. The wilderness lies in the Ochoco National Forest, within the South Fork John Day River’s drainage basin. Along the byway, the river cuts through Columbia River basalt, with ponderosa pine, Douglas fir, white fir and willows beside the drive.

moments.title: Izee
moments.text: Izee takes its name from a cattle brand: a local rancher marked his animals with the letters I. Z. The ranching community stands on the South Fork John Day River. Its post office operated from 1889 to 1954. The small, two-room schoolhouse continued teaching children until 1989. Its use changed after the last students left: the building now serves community functions.

practical: Dayville: Some stretches are single-vehicle width. There is no cell phone service along the byway. (checked 2026-10-11)
